s1007.core: FIELD STAFF are ⟦0⟧volunteers present in and around the ARENA that are responsible for making sure the MATCHES are cycled through efficiently, fairly, safely, and with a spirit of cooperation, ⟦1⟧Gracious Professionalism⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧®⟦/4⟧⟦/3⟧⟦/2⟧, and generosity of spirit.

s1008.core: FIELD STAFF roles are filled by volunteers from the community who prepare for the event with thorough training and certification. There are 3 FIELD-side key volunteer roles with whom teams should be familiar with and are encouraged to use as resources to make their event experience valuable.⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧

s1009.core: - ⟦0⟧Head REFEREE⟦/0⟧ – trains, directs, and supervises REFEREES and Official Scorers. They oversee all scoring processes and procedures in collaboration with other FIELD STAFF. They interact with STUDENTS, volunteers, and event staff. The Head REFEREE has final authority for decisions regarding MATCH scores, FOULS, and YELLOW and RED CARD assignments. ⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧

s1010.core: ⟦0⟧- ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧FIRST⟦/2⟧ Technical Advisor ⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦3⟧(FTA)⟦/3⟧ - ensures events run smoothly, safely, and in accordance with ⟦4⟧FIRST⟦/4⟧ requirements. The FTA collaborates with ⟦5⟧FIRST⟦/5⟧ staff, event staff, and other event volunteers in many different areas at events. The FTA focuses on all technical things related to the FIELD, ROBOTS, and game, and acts as a team advocate for all teams competing at the event. ⟦6⟧⟦/6⟧

s1011.core: - ⟦0⟧FIELD Supervisor⟦/0⟧ - (may be the same as the FTA or Head REFEREE at smaller events) directs activity on the FIELD to ensure efficient execution of the MATCHES, pacing of the event, and smooth flow of MATCH play. FIELD Supervisors are responsible for ensuring the FIELD is intact and lead FIELD reset teams, who are responsible for resetting the FIELD after each MATCH in preparation for the subsequent MATCH. ⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧

s1012.core: For additional details about each of these roles, as well as other ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ Tech Challenge volunteer roles, please refer to the ⟦2⟧volunteer resources⟦/2⟧. ⟦3⟧⟦/3⟧

s1014.core: The ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ event management system is the software responsible for managing the MATCH scores and other event inputs. The system encompasses all FIELD electronics, including computers, displays, REFEREE, and other volunteer electronic devices, wireless access point, ethernet cables, etc.

s1015.core: The ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ event management system alerts participants to milestones in the MATCH using audio cues detailed in Table 9‑1. Please note that audio cues are intended as a courtesy to participants and not intended as official MATCH markers. If there is a discrepancy between an audio cue and the visual FIELD timers, the visual FIELD timers are the authority.

s1039.core: In BIOBUZZ, 2 ALLIANCES (an ALLIANCE is ⟦0⟧a cooperative of 2 ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ Tech Challenge teams⟦/0⟧) play MATCHES, set up and implemented per the details described below.

s1041.core: MATCHES consist of pre-MATCH setup, ⟦0⟧a 30-second AUTO period, an 8-second transition period between AUTO and TELEOP, and a 2-minute TELEOP period⟦/0⟧, followed by the post-MATCH reset.

s1042.core: During the MATCH, ROBOTS collect POLLEN and NECTAR to move them to their GARDEN, to place into the FLOWERS, and to LAUNCH them into their CELLS to cause a HIVE TIP – all to earn points.

s1043.core: Each time a HIVE is TIPPED, an ALLIANCE is allowed to enter one of five NECTAR initially staged in the ALLIANCE AREA. With 60 seconds left in the MATCH, ALLIANCES can enter all remaining NECTAR.

s1044.core: ROBOTS conclude the MATCH by claiming ownership of the FLOWERS by placing NECTAR and returning to their LOADING ZONE.

s1046.core: A DRIVE TEAM is ⟦0⟧a set of up to 4 people from the same ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ Tech Challenge team responsible for team performance for a specific MATCH⟦/0⟧. There are 3 specific roles on a DRIVE TEAM which ALLIANCES can use to assist ROBOTS, and only 1 member of the DRIVE TEAM is allowed to be a non-STUDENT.

s1047.core: The intent of the definition of DRIVE TEAM and DRIVE TEAM related rules is that, barring extenuating circumstances, the DRIVE TEAM consists of people who arrived at the event affiliated with that team and are responsible for their team’s and ROBOT’S performance at the event (this means a person may be affiliated with more than 1 team).

s1048.core: The intent is not to allow teams to “adopt” members of other teams for STRATEGIC advantage for the loaning team, borrowing team, and/or their ALLIANCE (e.g., an ALLIANCE Lead believes 1 of their DRIVERS has more experience than a DRIVER of their ALLIANCE partner, and the teams agree the partner team will “adopt” that DRIVER and make them a member of their DRIVE TEAM for Playoffs).

s1049.core: The definition is not stricter for 2 main reasons. First, to avoid additional bureaucratic burden on teams and event volunteers (e.g., requiring that teams submit official rosters that Queuing must check before allowing a DRIVE TEAM into the ARENA). Second, to provide space for exceptional circumstances that give teams the opportunity to display ⟦1⟧Gracious Professionalism⟦/1⟧ (e.g., a bus is delayed, a DRIVE COACH has no DRIVERS, and their pit neighbors agree to help by loaning DRIVERS as temporary members of the team until their bus arrives).

s1058.core: any team member and may be an adult, must wear “DRIVE COACH” badge

s1060.core: an operator and controller of the ROBOT

s1061.core: STUDENT, must wear a “DRIVE TEAM” badge

s1064.core: A STUDENT is ⟦0⟧a person who has not completed high-school, secondary school, or the comparable level in their HOME REGION as of September 1⟦1⟧st⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧ of the current season.

s1066.core: Before each MATCH begins, FIELD STAFF stage SCORING ELEMENTS as described in Section ⟦0⟧10.3.1⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧SCORING ELEMENTS⟦/2⟧. DRIVE TEAMS stage their ROBOTS (as described in Section ⟦3⟧10.3.4⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧ ⟦/4⟧⟦5⟧ROBOTS⟦/5⟧) and OPERATOR CONSOLES (as described in Section ⟦6⟧10.3.3⟦/6⟧⟦7⟧ ⟦/7⟧⟦8⟧OPERATOR CONSOLES⟦/8⟧). Then, DRIVE TEAMS take their places as described in Section ⟦9⟧⟦/9⟧⟦10⟧⟦/10⟧⟦11⟧⟦/11⟧⟦12⟧⟦/12⟧⟦13⟧⟦/13⟧⟦14⟧⟦/14⟧⟦15⟧⟦/15⟧⟦16⟧⟦/16⟧⟦17⟧⟦/17⟧⟦18⟧10.3.2⟦/18⟧⟦19⟧ ⟦/19⟧⟦20⟧DRIVE TEAMS⟦/20⟧.

s1069.core: Each HIVE is tilted such that one CELL is pointed down, and the other CELL is pointed up, as shown. (An easy way to remember this is the CELL which “points at” a FLOWER should be the one tilted down.) SCORING ELEMENTS are staged on the FIELD as follows (Figure 10‑2):

s1070.core: A. 40 POLLEN are staged on the FIELD as follows:

s1071.core: i. 4 POLLEN in each of the 4 FLOWERS (16)

s1072.core: ii. 4 POLLEN in the red GARDEN (4)

s1073.core: iii. 4 POLLEN in the blue GARDEN (4)

s1074.core: iv. 4 POLLEN pre-loaded in each ROBOT (16) (Section ⟦0⟧10.3.4⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧ROBOTS⟦/2⟧)

s1075.core: Pre-loaded POLLEN start the MATCH located in or on the ROBOT, or on the TILES contacting the ROBOT. ROBOTS that are not present for their MATCH will have their pre-load POLLEN placed in approximately the center of the LOADING ZONE against the perimeter wall.

s1076.core: POLLEN in the GARDEN is placed in a line starting in the corner closest to the ALLIANCE AREA and contacting the audience or rear perimeter wall. Some minor variance in placement may occur.

s1077.core: B. 8 red and 8 blue NECTAR are staged on the FIELD as follows:

s1078.core: i. 3 NECTAR in each upward-facing CELL of corresponding color (6)

s1079.core: ii. 5 NECTAR are in each ALLIANCE AREA of corresponding color (10)

s1080.core: NECTAR in the CELL is placed contacting the back wall of the CELL and in a line against the side closest to the ALLIANCE AREA of corresponding color. There may be some variation in where these NECTAR are placed by volunteers, but they will be generally placed as shown.

s1081.core: As described in ⟦0⟧15.2⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧Game Modification⟦/2⟧: the number, type, and distribution of SCORING ELEMENTS may be adjusted for the ⟦3⟧FIRST⟦/3⟧ Championship and ⟦4⟧FIRST⟦/4⟧ Premier Events. For the ⟦5⟧FIRST⟦/5⟧ Championship, any game modifications will be published on or before the last regularly scheduled Team Update as described in Section ⟦6⟧1.7.3⟦/6⟧⟦7⟧ ⟦/7⟧⟦8⟧Team Updates⟦/8⟧. For ⟦9⟧FIRST⟦/9⟧ Premier Events, game modifications will be posted by the event organizers prior to the event.

s1083.core: DRIVE TEAMS prepare for a MATCH by staging in the ALLIANCE AREA after the DRIVE TEAM from the previous MATCH has left. DRIVE TEAM starting conditions are listed below, and a DRIVE TEAM obstructing or delaying any of the conditions is at risk of violating ⟦0⟧G301⟦/0⟧.

s1084.core: A. Only DRIVE TEAM members assigned to the upcoming MATCH are present.

s1085.core: B. Only DRIVE TEAM members whose ROBOTS have passed initial, complete inspection are present.

s1086.core: C. DRIVE TEAM members are staged in their designated ALLIANCE AREA. If members of the ALLIANCE cannot agree where their DRIVE TEAM members will be staged, the team listed on the MATCH schedule as “Red 1” or “Blue 1” will stage closest to the audience.

s1087.core: D. DRIVE TEAM members clearly display their designated DRIVE TEAM badges above their waists.

s1088.core: E. If a Playoff MATCH, the ALLIANCE CAPTAIN clearly displays their designated ALLIANCE CAPTAIN identifier (e.g., hat, armband).

s1090.core: DRIVE TEAMS set up their OPERATOR CONSOLES as soon as they are staged in their ALLIANCE AREA. OPERATOR CONSOLES must be compliant with all relevant rules, specifically those in Section ⟦0⟧12.9⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧ ⟦/2⟧⟦/1⟧⟦3⟧OPERATOR CONSOLE⟦/3⟧. A DRIVE TEAM obstructing or delaying OPERATOR CONSOLE set up is at risk of violating ⟦4⟧G301⟦/4⟧.

s1091.core: A. DRIVE TEAMS intending to run an OpMode during AUTO must select an OpMode within their DRIVER STATION app with the 30 second timer enabled.

s1092.core: B. Otherwise, DRIVE TEAMS must select a TELEOP OpMode within the DRIVER STATION app.

s1093.core: C. The selected OpMode must be initialized by pressing the “INIT” button on the DRIVER STATION app.

s1095.core: DRIVE TEAMS stage their ROBOT in accordance with ⟦0⟧G304⟦/0⟧. A DRIVE TEAM obstructing or delaying ROBOT setup requirements is at risk of violating ⟦1⟧G301⟦/1⟧.

s1096.core: ROBOTS must start the MATCH contacting 4 pre-loaded POLLEN. POLLEN may be held in or on a ROBOT or placed on the TILES fully contained on its own ALLIANCE side of the FIELD contacting the ROBOT in its starting location.

s1097.core: If a ROBOT is DISABLED prior to the start of a MATCH, it can be removed from the FIELD in coordination with FIELD STAFF. A team whose ROBOT is DISABLED or not present is eligible to receive Qualification MATCH Points or Playoff MATCH points provided that its ROBOT has passed inspection per Section ⟦0⟧3.3.1⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧Inspection⟦/2⟧, and as long as at least one STUDENT DRIVE TEAM member is present in the ALLIANCE AREA

s1098.core: If order of placement matters to either or both ALLIANCES, the ALLIANCE notifies the Head REFEREE or their designee before setting up for that MATCH, and the Head REFEREE instructs ALLIANCES to alternate placement of ROBOTS. REFEREE instructions are that ROBOTS are placed in the following order:

s1103.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧In Qualification MATCHES, the ROBOT assigned to Red 1 or Blue 1 places first within their ALLIANCE. In Playoff MATCHES, the ALLIANCE lead decides which ROBOT places first within their ALLIANCE.

s1105.core: The first period of each MATCH is 30 seconds (0:30) long and called the Autonomous Period (AUTO). During AUTO, ROBOTS operate without any DRIVER control or input.

s1106.core: There is an 8-second transition period between AUTO and TELEOP for scoring purposes as described in Section ⟦0⟧10.5⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧Scoring⟦/2⟧.

s1107.core: The ⟦0⟧third period of each MATCH is 2 minutes (2:00) long and called the teleoperated period (TELEOP). During TELEOP, DRIVERS remotely operate ROBOTS⟦/0⟧ to score points. See Table 9‑1 for detailed MATCH timing.

s1109.core: ALLIANCES are rewarded for accomplishing various actions throughout a MATCH as shown in Table 10‑2.

s1110.core: ALLIANCES are rewarded for their performance during MATCHES via MATCH points and RANKING POINTS (RP), which increase the measure used to rank teams per Section ⟦0⟧13.6.3⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧Qualification Ranking⟦/2⟧.

s1111.core: All achievements are updated throughout the MATCH. Scoring achievements are assessed as follows:

s1112.core: A. Assessment of HIVE TIPS occurs throughout the MATCH and continues until all SCORING ELEMENTS and ROBOTS have come to rest at the conclusion of the MATCH.

s1113.core: B. HIVE TIPS that are complete prior to the start of TELEOP are assessed as part of AUTO.

s1114.core: C. Assessment of POLLEN and NECTAR remaining in the CELL will occur after all SCORING ELEMENTS and ROBOTS have come to rest at the conclusion of the MATCH.

s1115.core: D. Assessment of SCORING ELEMENTS scored in a FLOWER will occur throughout the MATCH with final assessment taking place at the end of TELEOP after all SCORING ELEMENTS and ROBOTS have come to rest at the conclusion of the MATCH.

s1116.core: E. Assessment of GARDEN scoring occurs at the end of TELEOP when all ROBOTS and SCORING ELEMENTS have come to rest at the conclusion of the MATCH.

s1117.core: F. Assessment of LEAVE and AUTO PARK occurs at the end of AUTO.

s1118.core: G. Assessment of TELEOP PARK occurs at the end of the MATCH.

s1123.core: The HIVE is considered TIPPED when:

s1124.core: A. it ⟦0⟧moves from one stable state to the other stable state with the downwards-facing CELL becoming the upwards-facing CELL⟦/0⟧, and

s1125.core: B. subsequently, ⟦0⟧the damper on the HIVE that was previously not contacting the frame begins to contact the frame⟦/0⟧.

s1127.core: The HIVES are designed to be bi-stable, and it should be obvious in most circumstances that a HIVE has moved from one stable state to the other. s1259.core: There are several styles of violation wording used in this manual. Below are some example violations and a clarification of the way the violation would be assessed. The examples shown do not represent all possible violations, but rather a representative set of combinations.

s1264.core: Upon instance of violation, a MINOR FOUL is assessed against the violating ALLIANCE.

s1266.core: Upon instance of violation, a MINOR FOUL is assessed against the violating ALLIANCE equal to the number of SCORING ELEMENTS used in violation of the rule.

s1267.core: MAJOR FOUL per instance. MAJOR FOUL per instance and YELLOW CARD per MATCH if REPEATED.

s1268.core: Upon initial violation in a MATCH, a MAJOR FOUL is assessed against the violating ALLIANCE per instance of a violation occurring.

s1269.core: If the condition of REPEATED in the second statement is met – i.e., the ROBOT repeats the infraction an additional time in the MATCH, then an additional MAJOR FOUL is assessed against the violating ALLIANCE for the subsequent instance of violation and after the MATCH, the violating team is issued a YELLOW CARD for the subsequent instance of violation.

s1270.core: Assuming no additional infractions of that rule by that ROBOT in that MATCH, the ROBOT is assessed two MAJOR FOULS and a YELLOW CARD for their team in that MATCH. Additional violations of this rule during the MATCH would increase the number of MAJOR FOULS assessed during the MATCH but not the number of YELLOW CARDS issued for the MATCH.

s1271.core: MAJOR FOUL and an additional MAJOR FOUL for every 3 seconds in which the situation is not corrected

s1272.core: Upon violation, a MAJOR FOUL is assessed against the violating ALLIANCE and the REFEREE begins to count. Their count continues until the criteria to discontinue the count are met, and for each 3 seconds within that time, an additional MAJOR FOUL is assessed against the violating ALLIANCE. A ROBOT in violation of this type of rule for 15 seconds is assessed a total of 6 MAJOR FOULS (assuming no other rules were being simultaneously violated).

s1273.core: VERBAL WARNING. MAJOR FOUL and YELLOW CARD per MATCH, if STRATEGIC.

s1274.core: Upon a general violation of the rule, a VERBAL WARNING is issued to the violating team. However, if the violation is perceived to be STRATEGIC by the REFEREES, then a MAJOR FOUL is assessed against the violating ALLIANCE and after the MATCH, the violating team is issued a YELLOW CARD.

s1278.core: Only 1 MAJOR FOUL and up to 1 YELLOW CARD can be earned by a team in a single MATCH.

s1339.core: A. ⟦0⟧a red ALLIANCE ROBOT deliberately drives into a blue ALLIANCE ROBOT that is lined up to score NECTAR into a FLOWER with 65 seconds left in the MATCH, causing them drop the NECTAR into the FLOWER early in violation of ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G410⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧.⟦/2⟧

s1340.core: B. ⟦0⟧a red ALLIANCE ROBOT drives through the blue LOADING ZONE while a blue DRIVE TEAM member is introducing NECTAR to the FIELD, deflecting the blue NECTAR before it contacts the TILE in the LOADING ZONE, in violation of ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G427⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧.⟦/2⟧

s1341.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧G205 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*Egregious or exceptional violations.⟦/3⟧ Egregious behavior beyond what is listed in the rules or subsequent violations of any rule or procedure during the event is prohibited.

s1342.core: In addition to rule violations explicitly listed in this manual and witnessed by a REFEREE, the Head REFEREE may assign a YELLOW or RED CARD for egregious ROBOT actions or team member behavior at any time during the event.

s1343.core: Continued violations will be brought to ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ Headquarters’ attention. ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ Headquarters will work with event staff to determine if further escalations are necessary, which can include removal from award consideration and removal from the event.

s1344.core: Deliberately violating a rule because the benefit of the violation outweighs the penalty is not in the spirit of ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ and is an example of egregious behavior. For example, multiple violations of rules without an escalation path because the cumulative benefit outweighs the cumulative penalty. Violating a rule that only results in a YELLOW CARD in an ALLIANCE’S potential last MATCH prior to cards clearing per Section ⟦1⟧10.6.1⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧ ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧YELLOW and RED CARDS⟦/3⟧ or the end of an event (such as a team’s last qualification MATCH, a lower bracket MATCH) will be under increased scrutiny and will likely result in a RED CARD.

s1345.core: Please see Section ⟦0⟧10.6.1⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧YELLOW and RED CARDS⟦/2⟧ for additional detail.

s1347.core: The intent of this rule is to provide the Head REFEREES with the flexibility necessary to keep the event running smoothly, as well as keep the safety of all the participants as the highest priority.

s1348.core: The Head REFEREE may assign a YELLOW or RED CARD for a single instance of a rule violation or for multiple instances of any single rule violation. Teams should be aware that any rule in this manual could escalate to a YELLOW or RED CARD. The Head REFEREE has final authority on all rules and violations at an event.

s1350.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧G301 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*Don’t delay MATCHES. ⟦/3⟧DRIVE TEAM members may not cause significant delays to the start of their MATCH. Both of these conditions must be met prior to team actions being considered:

s1351.core: A. the expected MATCH start time has passed, and

s1352.core: B. the DRIVE TEAM has access to the ARENA.

s1353.core: In order for a team to cause a significant delay, the Head REFEREE must perceive that the team is neither MATCH ready (⟦0⟧G303⟦/0⟧) nor making a good faith effort to quickly become MATCH ready.

s1354.core: During Qualification MATCHES, the expected start time of the MATCH is the time indicated on the MATCH schedule or ~3 minutes after the end of the previous MATCH on the same FIELD, whichever is later.

s1355.core: During Playoff MATCHES, the expected start time of the MATCH is the time indicated on the MATCH schedule or 8 minutes from either ALLIANCE’S previous MATCH, whichever is later

s1356.core: ⟦0⟧During back-to-back MATCHES, ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧T406⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧ is in effect, and teams may have a longer minimum break.⟦/2⟧

s1357.core: Teams that have 1 DRIVE TEAM member present and have informed FIELD STAFF that their ROBOT will not be participating in the MATCH are considered MATCH ready and not in violation of this rule.

s1358.core: Violation: VERBAL WARNING. MAJOR FOUL for the upcoming MATCH if a subsequent violation occurs within the tournament phase. In a Playoff MATCH, the VERBAL WARNING is issued to the entire ALLIANCE.

s1359.core: If the team/ALLIANCE is not MATCH ready within 2 minutes of the VERBAL WARNING/MAJOR FOUL having been issued, and the Head REFEREE perceives no good faith effort by the DRIVE TEAM(S) to quickly become MATCH ready, the offending team’s ROBOT is DISABLED.

s1360.core: The intent of this rule is to provide an equitable amount of time for both ALLIANCES to prepare for each MATCH and give DRIVE TEAMS grace given extenuating circumstances that cause them to be late. Teams should avoid disrupting ARENA operations and proactively communicate with the Head REFEREE and FIELD STAFF to let them know their status.

s1361.core: FIELD STAFF will make a good faith effort to wait for missing or unprepared teams and will avoid beginning any MATCH when teams are not present or not MATCH ready and making good faith effort to become MATCH ready.

s1362.core: Once a VERBAL WARNING/MAJOR FOUL is issued, the Head REFEREE starts a 2-minute timer and makes a good faith effort to share the timer’s status with the delaying DRIVE TEAM.

s1363.core: In general, good faith efforts to quickly become MATCH ready are entirely for the purposes of transitioning the ROBOT into a MATCH ready state (i.e., not attempts to significantly alter a ROBOT’S capabilities). Examples of good faith efforts to quickly become MATCH ready that would not be a violation include but are not limited to:

s1364.core: A. ⟦0⟧walking safely towards the FIELD with a ROBOT that a team is not actively modifying,⟦/0⟧

s1365.core: B. ⟦0⟧applying quick fixes such as tape or cable ties to make the ROBOT compliant with STARTING CONFIGURATION requirements,⟦/0⟧

s1366.core: C. ⟦0⟧waiting for a DRIVER STATION device to boot,⟦/0⟧

s1367.core: D. ⟦0⟧actively working with field technical staff, including the FTA, to resolve an issue in a reasonable amount of time, or ⟦/0⟧

s1368.core: E. ⟦0⟧performing a MOMENTARY “wiggle test” to confirm communication between the DRIVER STATION and the ROBOT CONTROLLER. The ROBOT should not drive or interact with SCORING ELEMENTS (except contact with pre-loaded POLLEN) while performing this test. ⟦/0⟧

s1369.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧G302 ⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧*Limit what you bring to the FIELD⟦/4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧.⟦/6⟧⟦/5⟧⟦7⟧⟦8⟧ ⟦/8⟧⟦/7⟧Items brought to the FIELD to be used for a MATCH, in addition to the ROBOT and OPERATOR CONSOLE, must fit in the team’s designated ALLIANCE AREA, be worn or held by members of the DRIVE TEAM, or be an item used as an accommodation (e.g., crutches, cushions, kneeling mats, or single-step stools no more than 12 in. tall (30.5 cm) that are designed to be stood on and are locked such that they do not roll/fold).

s1370.core: Regardless of whether the equipment fits the criteria above, it may not:

s1371.core: A. be employed in a way that disrupts normal ARENA operations or introduces a safety hazard,

s1372.core: B. extend more than 6 ft. 6 in. (~198 cm) above the TILES,

s1373.core: C. communicate with anything or anyone outside of the ARENA with the exception of medically required equipment,

s1374.core: D. block visibility for FIELD STAFF or audience members, or

s1375.core: E. jam or interfere with the remote sensing capabilities of another team.

s1376.core: Exceptions to ⟦0⟧G302⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧.⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧B⟦/2⟧ are granted for MOMENTARY extensions above 6 ft. 6in. and for individuals wearing PPE or reasonable decorative apparel such as hats, headbands, etc.

s1377.core: Violation: MATCH will not start until the situation is remedied. VERBAL WARNING, if discovered or used inappropriately during a MATCH. YELLOW CARD if subsequent violations occur during the event.

s1378.core: ⟦0⟧It is not a violation of this rule to bring an alignment device to the FIELD to aid pre-MATCH ROBOT set-up and alignment. The use of any alignment devices should not delay MATCH start in violation of ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G301⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧.⟦/2⟧

s1379.core: Examples of equipment that may be considered a safety hazard in the confined space of the ALLIANCE AREA include but are not limited to: a ladder or a large signaling device.

s1380.core: ⟦0⟧Using an item that has wireless communications disabled complies with ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G302⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧.C⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧ above. ⟦/3⟧

s1381.core: Examples of jamming or interfering with remote sensing capabilities include but are not limited to: mimicking the FIELD AprilTags and shining bright lighting or laser pointers onto the FIELD during a MATCH.

s1382.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧G303 ⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧*ROBOTS on the FIELD must come ready to play a MATCH.⟦/4⟧ A ROBOT must meet all following MATCH-start requirements:

s1383.core: A. does not pose a hazard to humans, ARENA elements, or other ROBOTS,

s1384.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧B. meets all the requirements from Section ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧3.3⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧ ⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧MATCH Eligibility Rules⟦/4⟧ including those regarding inspection/re-inspection,

s1385.core: C. is the only team-provided item left in the FIELD, and

s1386.core: D. has ROBOT SIGNS that indicate the correct ALLIANCE color (see ⟦0⟧R402⟦/0⟧).

DISABLED if it is not a quick remedy, and, at the discretion of the Head REFEREE, ROBOT must be re-inspected. RED CARD if a team’s ROBOT is not compliant with ⟦0⟧G303⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧.⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧B⟦/2⟧ participates in the MATCH.

s1388.core: For assessment of many of the items listed above, the Head REFEREE is likely to consult with the LRI.

These pre-load POLLEN are specifically allocated as 4 for each team as described in Section ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧10.3.1⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧ ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧SCORING ELEMENTS⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧. s1403.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G305 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Teams must select an OpMode.⟦/2⟧ An OpMode must be selected on the DRIVER STATION app and initialized by pressing the INIT button. If this OpMode is an AUTO OpMode, the 30 second AUTO timer must be enabled.

s1404.core: Violation: MATCH will not start until the situation is remedied. DISABLED if ROBOT cannot initialize an OpMode or the situation cannot be remedied quickly.

s1405.core: This rule requires all teams to select and INIT an OpMode, regardless of whether or not an AUTO OpMode is planned to be used during AUTO. FIELD STAFF will use this as an indication that a team is ready to start the MATCH.

s1408.core: Rules in this section pertain to gameplay once a MATCH begins.

s1411.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G401 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Don’t interact with a ROBOT during AUTO.⟦/2⟧ As soon as the countdown to start the MATCH begins and until the end of AUTO, DRIVE TEAM members may not directly or indirectly interact with a ROBOT or an OPERATOR CONSOLE, with the following exceptions:

s1413.core: B. to press the (■) stop button at the team’s discretion, or

s1414.core: C. for personal safety or OPERATOR CONSOLE safety.

s1416.core: Teams do not have to start an OpMode if they choose not to run an AUTO OpMode.

s1417.core: ⟦0⟧The intent of ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G401⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧.A⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧ is for teams to start AUTO on time, accounting for some variability due to human factors.⟦/3⟧

s1418.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧G402 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧No AUTO opponent interference. ⟦/3⟧During AUTO, a team may not disrupt AUTO for the opposing ALLIANCE.

s1419.core: Violation: MAJOR FOUL per MATCH. MAJOR FOUL and YELLOW CARD per MATCH, if STRATEGIC.

s1420.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧During AUTO, FIELD columns A, B, C constitute the red side of the FIELD, and columns D, E, F (⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧Figure 9‑5⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧) constitute the blue side of the FIELD. Each ALLIANCE has priority over those FIELD and SCORING ELEMENTS on their side of the FIELD.⟦/4⟧⟦/3⟧

s1421.core: Navigating into the opposing ALLIANCE’S side of the FIELD during AUTO is a risky gameplay strategy that may be seen as STRATEGIC.

s1422.core: Examples of actions that are considered disruption of AUTO include but are not limited to:

s1423.core: ⟦0⟧A. ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧CONTROLLING SCORING ELEMENTS located on the opposing ALLIANCE’S side of the FIELD, and ⟦/2⟧⟦/1⟧

s1424.core: ⟦0⟧B. ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧contact an opposing ROBOT on their side of the FIELD.⟦/2⟧⟦/1⟧

s1427.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧G403 ⟦/2⟧⟦/1⟧⟦3⟧*ROBOTS are motionless between AUTO and TELEOP.⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧⟦5⟧ Any powered movement of the ROBOT or any of its MECHANISMS is not allowed during the transition period between AUTO and TELEOP.⟦/5⟧⟦/4⟧

s1428.core: Violation: VERBAL WARNING. MAJOR FOUL and YELLOW CARD per MATCH, if STRATEGIC.

s1429.core: Movement due to inertia, gravity, or de-energizing of actuators, etc. is not considered powered movement.

s1430.core: Teams may press buttons on their DRIVER STATION app to stop the AUTO OpMode, initialize or start a TELEOP OpMode during the AUTO to TELEOP transition period. If the INIT portion of the OpMode causes the ROBOT to violate this rule (powering actuators such that they move or twitch in any way), then the team should wait until TELEOP begins before pressing INIT.

s1431.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧G404 ⟦/2⟧⟦/1⟧⟦3⟧*ROBOTS are motionless at the end of TELEOP⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧⟦5⟧.⟦/5⟧⟦/4⟧⟦6⟧⟦7⟧ ⟦/7⟧⟦/6⟧⟦8⟧⟦9⟧ROBOTS must no longer have powered movement after the end of TELEOP until the Head REFEREE or their designee signals that teams may retrieve their ROBOTS. ⟦/9⟧⟦/8⟧

s1432.core: Violation: VERBAL WARNING. MAJOR FOUL and YELLOW CARD per MATCH, if STRATEGIC.

s1437.core: Violation: MAJOR FOUL per SCORING ELEMENT.

s1439.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧G406 ⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧*Do not damage or make a mess in the ARENA.⟦/4⟧ Neither a ROBOT nor a DRIVE TEAM member may make a mess or damage any part of the ARENA.

s1440.core: Violation: VERBAL WARNING. MAJOR FOUL and YELLOW CARD per MATCH, if STRATEGIC. DISABLED if the damage is caused by a ROBOT, and the Head REFEREE perceives that further damage is likely to occur.

s1441.core: Corrective action (such as eliminating sharp edges, removing the damaging MECHANISM, and/or reinspection) may be required before the ROBOT may compete in subsequent MATCHES.

s1442.core: ⟦0⟧The intent of this rule is that DRIVE TEAM members and ROBOTS negatively impact the ARENA, including FIELD elements and SCORING ELEMENTS in a way that would result in significant repair or extensive cleanup that disrupts ARENA operations. Rule ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R201⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧ describes examples of ROBOT features related to this rule that are scrutinized during inspection.⟦/2⟧

s1443.core: SCORING ELEMENTS are expected to undergo a reasonable amount of wear and tear as they are handled by ROBOTS and humans, such as scratching, marking, and eventually damage due to fatigue. Routinely gouging, tearing off pieces, or marking SCORING ELEMENTS are violations of this rule.

s1444.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧G407 ⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧No more than 4 at a time.⟦/4⟧ A ROBOT may not simultaneously CONTROL more than 4 SCORING ELEMENTS.

s1445.core: Violation: VERBAL WARNING. MAJOR FOUL and YELLOW CARD per MATCH, if STRATEGIC.

s1446.core: The intent of this rule is that ROBOTS play MATCHES while only CONTROLLING a maximum of 4 SCORING ELEMENTS at a time.

s1447.core: ROBOTS that CONTROL 5 or more SCORING ELEMENTS at any time during the MATCH will be under scrutiny to determine whether it is STRATEGIC.

s1448.core: Examples of actions that are likely to be perceived as STRATEGIC include, but are not limited to:

s1449.core: A. ⟦0⟧A ROBOT that picks up and CONTROLS 6 or more SCORING ELEMENTS, moving them to a scoring location.⟦/0⟧

s1450.core: B. ⟦0⟧Multiple instances of greater than MOMENTARY CONTROL of 5 or more SCORING ELEMENTS by a ROBOT throughout a MATCH. ⟦/0⟧

s1451.core: Examples of actions that are likely to ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧not⟦/2⟧⟦/1⟧ be perceived as STRATEGIC include, but are not limited to:

s1452.core: C. ⟦0⟧A ROBOT MOMENTARILY CONTROLS 5 SCORING ELEMENTS which they “reverse” quickly so that at least one SCORING ELEMENT returns to approximately its original state. ⟦/0⟧

s1453.core: Teams are encouraged to design their ROBOTS to prevent inadvertent or deliberate CONTROL of more than 4 SCORING ELEMENTS. This could involve guards to prevent SCORING ELEMENTS from accidentally becoming stuck on top of the ROBOT and systems to prevent active pickup/intaking of more than 4 SCORING ELEMENTS.

s1454.core: REPEATED instances of a ROBOT CONTROLLING 5 or more SCORING ELEMENTS are likely to be perceived as STRATEGIC, even if the ROBOT has a “keep 4 and discard the rest” sorting mechanism.

s1455.core: Examples of interaction with a SCORING ELEMENT that are not “CONTROL” and would not be a violation of this rule include, but are not limited to:

s1457.core: E. ⟦0⟧“deflecting” (being hit by a SCORING ELEMENT that bounces into or off a ROBOT), or⟦/0⟧

s1514.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧G417 ⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧ROBOTS may not meddle with the HIVE Structure.⟦/4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ ⟦/6⟧⟦/5⟧ROBOTS may not manipulate the motion of the HIVE in any way other than by LAUNCHING SCORING ELEMENTS into an upward-facing CELL.

s1527.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧G418 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧ROBOTS may not meddle with FLOWERS.⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ ⟦/4⟧⟦/3⟧ROBOTS may not enter SCORING ELEMENTS into or remove SCORING ELEMENTS from a FLOWER except:

Any other actions to score or remove SCORING ELEMENTS from the FLOWER are considered a violation of this rule.

s1548.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧G419 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*Do not damage an opponent ROBOT.⟦/3⟧ A ROBOT may not damage or functionally impair an opponent ROBOT.

s1550.core: BIOBUZZ is a highly interactive game and may include defensive and high-contact gameplay. While this rule prevents teams from damaging their opponents STRATEGICALLY and aims to limit severe damage to ROBOTS, teams should design their ROBOTS to be robust.

s1551.core: The damage or functional impairment of exposed or unprotected COMPONENTS or MECHANISMS in the course of normal gameplay is not likely to be considered a violation of this rule. This includes, but is not limited to:

s1552.core: A. ⟦0⟧an exposed or unprotected main power switch (see ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R603⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧),⟦/2⟧

s1554.core: C. ⟦0⟧a delicately constructed MECHANISM (such as an intake).⟦/0⟧

s1555.core: When a team’s ROBOT is interacting with an opponent ROBOT that is in a precarious or disadvantaged position, that team should make it obvious and unambiguous that they are trying to avoid damaging their opponent.

s1556.core: Examples of actions that are likely to be perceived as STRATEGIC include, but are not limited to:

s1557.core: D. ⟦0⟧A ROBOT high-speed rams and/or REPEATEDLY smashes an opponent ROBOT and causes damage.⟦/0⟧

s1558.core: Examples of functionally impairing another ROBOT include, but are not limited to:

s1559.core: E. ⟦0⟧disconnecting wires inside the ROBOT CHASSIS required for operation of a COMPONENT,⟦/0⟧

s1560.core: F. ⟦0⟧disconnecting the opponent ROBOT’S battery (this is also an example of a ROBOT no longer able to drive), or⟦/0⟧

s1561.core: G. ⟦0⟧powering off an opponent’s ROBOT by contacting their reasonably well-protected power switch. (This is also an example of a ROBOT no longer able to drive.)⟦/0⟧

s1575.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧G421 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*There is a 3-count on PINS. ⟦/3⟧A ROBOT may not PIN an opponent’s ROBOT for more than 3 seconds. s1639.core: ROBOTS are made up of COMPONENTS and MECHANISMS.

s1640.core: - A COMPONENT is ⟦0⟧any part in its most basic configuration, which cannot be disassembled without damaging or destroying the part or altering its fundamental function⟦/0⟧.

s1642.core: Many rules in this section reference Commercial-Off-The-Shelf (COTS) items. A COTS item must be ⟦0⟧a standard (i.e., not custom order) part commonly available from a VENDOR for all teams for purchase⟦/0⟧. To be a COTS item, the COMPONENT or MECHANISM must be in an unaltered, unmodified state (with the exception of installation or modification of any software). Items that are no longer commercially available but are functionally equivalent to the original condition as delivered from the VENDOR are considered COTS.

s1643.core: Example 1: A team orders 2 ROBOT panels from RoboPanels Corp. and receives both items. They put 1 in their storeroom and plan to use it later. Into the other, they drill “lightening holes” to reduce weight. The first panel is still classified as a COTS item, but the second panel is now a FABRICATED ITEM, as it has been modified.

s1644.core: Example 2: A team obtains openly available blueprints of a drive module commonly available from Wheels-R-Us Inc. and has local machine shop “We-Make-It, Inc.” manufacture a copy of the part for them. The produced part is not a COTS item, because it is not commonly carried as part of the standard stock of We-Make-It, Inc.

s1645.core: Example 3: A team obtains openly available design drawings from a professional publication and uses them to fabricate a gearbox for their ROBOT. The design drawings are considered a COTS item and may be used as “raw material” to fabricate the gearbox. The finished gearbox itself would be a FABRICATED ITEM, and not a COTS item.

s1646.core: Example 4: A COTS part that has non-functional label markings added would still be considered a COTS part, but a COTS part that has device-specific mounting holes added is a FABRICATED ITEM.

s1647.core: Example 5: A team has a COTS gearbox which has been discontinued. If the COTS gearbox is functionally equivalent to its original condition, it may be used.

s1648.core: A VENDOR is ⟦0⟧a legitimate business source for COTS items that satisfies⟦/0⟧ all the following criteria:

s1649.core: A. has a Federal Tax Identification number. In cases where the VENDOR is outside of the United States, they must possess an equivalent form of registration or license with the government of their home nation that establishes and validates their status as a legitimate business licensed to operate within that country.

s1650.core: B. is not a “wholly owned subsidiary” of a ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ team or collection of teams. While there may be some individuals affiliated with both a team and the VENDOR, the business and activities of the team and VENDOR must be completely separable.

s1651.core: C. should maintain sufficient stock or production capability so they are able to ship any general (i.e., non-⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ unique) product within a timely manner. It is recognized that certain unusual circumstances (such as a global supply chain disruption and/or 1,000 ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ teams all ordering the same part at once from the same VENDOR) may cause atypical delays in shipping due to backorders for even the largest VENDORS. Such delays due to higher-than-normal order rates are excused. This criterion may not apply to custom-built items from a source that is both a VENDOR and a fabricator.

s1652.core: For example, a VENDOR may sell flexible belting that the team wishes to procure to use as treads on their drive system. The VENDOR cuts the belting to a custom length from standard shelf stock that is typically available, welds it into a loop to make a tread, and ships it to a team. The fabrication of the tread takes the VENDOR 2 weeks. This would be considered a FABRICATED ITEM, and the 2-week ship time is acceptable. Alternately, the team may decide to fabricate the treads themselves. To satisfy this criterion, the VENDOR would just have to ship a length of belting from shelf stock (i.e., a COTS item) to the team within 5 business days and leave the welding of the cuts to the team.

s1653.core: D. makes their products available to all ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ Tech Challenge teams. A VENDOR must not limit supply or make a product available to just a limited number of ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ Tech Challenge teams.

s1654.core: The intent of this definition is to be as inclusive as possible to permit access to all legitimate sources, while preventing ad hoc organizations from providing special-purpose products to a limited subset of teams in an attempt to circumvent any applicable cost accounting rules.

s1655.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧ desires to permit teams to have the broadest choice of legitimate sources possible, and to obtain COTS items from the sources that provide them with the best prices and level of service available. Teams also need to protect against long delays in availability of parts that will impact their ability to complete their ROBOT. The build season is brief, so the VENDOR must be able to get their product, particularly ⟦3⟧FIRST⟦/3⟧ unique items, to a team in a timely manner. ⟦/2⟧

s1656.core: Ideally, chosen VENDORS should have effective distribution channels. Remember, ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ Tech Challenge events are not always near home – when parts fail, local access to replacement materials is often critical.

s1657.core: A FABRICATED ITEM is ⟦0⟧any COMPONENT or MECHANISM that has been altered, built, cast, constructed, concocted, created, cut, heat treated, machined, manufactured, modified, painted, produced, surface coated, or conjured partially or completely into the final form in which it will be used on the ROBOT⟦/0⟧.

(~152 cm) pieces by the team for storage or transport is neither COTS (it is not in the state received from the VENDOR), nor a FABRICATED ITEM (the cuts were not made to advance the part towards its final form on the ROBOT).

s1743.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧R303 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*COTS must be single DoF.⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧⟦5⟧ ⟦/5⟧⟦/4⟧COTS COMPONENTS and MECHANISMS must not exceed a single degree of mechanical freedom (DoF). Examples of allowed COTS single degree of freedom MECHANISMS and COMPONENTS are as follows:

s1751.core: Allowed exceptions to this rule are:

s1755.core: K. items that transfer motion between misaligned COMPONENTS (such as universal joints, flexible shaft couplers, and similar items), and

s1756.core: L. items that connect structures at variable angles (such as ball joint linkages, rod ends, and similar items).

s1757.core: The intent of this rule also extends to disallow highly specialized individual COMPONENTS only designed to assemble into a multiple DoF COTS COMPONENT.

s1758.core: The general test for a single degree of freedom MECHANISM is whether the orientation and position of each COMPONENT in the MECHANISM can be generally predicted based on the orientation and position of a single COMPONENT (such as the input) of the system.

s1759.core: Example 1: A mecanum drivetrain is made up of 4 independent drive modules, each with a single DoF (ignoring the DoF of the mecanum wheels as allowed by this rule), attached to a common structure (e.g., CHASSIS). The overall MECHANISM is still a single DoF.

s1760.core: Example 2: Dead wheel odometry modules, allowed by this rule, are typically composed of a 1 DoF wheel (ignoring the effect of the holonomic wheel) providing forward/backwards motion and a spring force providing an additional unique rotational or vertical motion, creating a 2 DoF system.

s1761.core: Example 3: Simple gripper claws, comprised of a single actuator moving 2 gripper jaws simultaneously or double actuators each controlling an independent gripper jaw, are by and large a single DoF. However, grippers that incorporate additional actuators providing additional twisting and/or bending actions (like a wrist) add degrees of freedom that are prohibited in COTS MECHANISMS.

s1765.core: A ROBOT SIGN is ⟦0⟧a required assembly which attaches to the ROBOT⟦/0⟧. A ROBOT SIGN ⟦1⟧simultaneously identifies a ROBOT’S team number as well as its ALLIANCE affiliation⟦/1⟧ for FIELD STAFF. Criteria used in writing these rules include the following:

s1766.core: - Maximize FIELD STAFF’S ability to determine team number and ALLIANCE of a ROBOT,

s1767.core: - Minimize the amount of design challenge in creating ROBOT SIGNS, and

s1768.core: - Increase consistency in displaying ROBOT identification.

s1769.core: A template ROBOT SIGN is available for download in ⟦0⟧US Letter⟦/0⟧ and ⟦1⟧A4⟦/1⟧ size.

These locations must be on opposite or adjacent surfaces of the ROBOT, ≥90 degrees apart. All ROBOT surfaces visible to FIELD STAFF can be used for placing ROBOT SIGNS including the top of the ROBOT. ROBOT SIGNS must meet the following criteria:

s1771.core: A. be made of a robust material,

s1772.core: B. minimally be 6.5 inches (16.5 cm) wide,

s1773.core: C. minimally be 2.5 inches (6.4 cm) tall (Figure 12‑7), and

s1774.core: D. be supported by the structure/frame of the ROBOT.

s1775.core: The intent of this rule is for FIELD STAFF to easily view ROBOT SIGNS from at least 12 feet (3.65 meters) away before, during, and after the MATCH.

s1776.core: ROBOT SIGNS should be robust enough to withstand the rigors of MATCH play, but there is no specific guidance on what is robust enough. Teams should make a good faith effort with whatever they have available.

(16.50 cm by 6.35 cm) in size to indicate their ALLIANCE color (Figure 12‑7), as assigned in the MATCH schedule at the event. Visible markings on ROBOT SIGNS when installed on the ROBOT, other than the following, are prohibited:

s1780.core: B. small amounts of hook-and-loop tape, hard fasteners, or functional equivalents,

s1781.core: C. narrow areas of differing colors exposed at corners, folds, or cutouts,

s1782.core: D. narrow markings on background solely for template purposes, and

s1783.core: E. cannot be powered or rely on power from any sources to illuminate/reveal ALLIANCE color.

s1784.core: ROBOT SIGNS that are reversible or configurable must not allow the opposite ALLIANCE color to be visible to FIELD STAFF, except where permitted by this rule.

s1869.core: E. insulation may be applied to electrical terminals,

s1870.core: F. repairs, provided the original performance and specifications are unchanged, and

s1871.core: G. maintenance recommended by the manufacturer.

s2016.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R612 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Do not modify critical power paths.⟦/2⟧ CUSTOM CIRCUITS must not directly alter the power or control pathways between:

s2017.core: A. the ROBOT battery and main power switch,

s2018.core: B. the main power switch and a power regulating device (per ⟦0⟧R603⟦/0⟧),

s2019.core: C. any two power regulating devices (per ⟦0⟧R607⟦/0⟧), or

s2021.core: Dynamic electrical interfaces (including linear sliding contacts) or continuous-rotation electrical interfaces (including slip rings) placed along any of these pathways must be unmodified COTS items; custom or fabricated electrical interfaces of this type are prohibited.

s2022.core: Custom high impedance voltage monitoring or low impedance current monitoring circuitry connected to the ROBOT’S electrical system is acceptable if the effect on power pathways is inconsequential.

s2023.core: Altering a power pathway includes, but is not limited to, altering the voltage of the power pathway using a boost (DC voltage step-up) or buck (DC voltage step-down) converter or otherwise altering the natural variable DC voltage provided by the ROBOT battery to create a constant DC voltage.

s2025.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R613 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Do not mix and match power on or between power regulation devices.⟦/2⟧ The following rules must be adhered to when using power on any power regulation device (per ⟦3⟧R505⟦/3⟧):

s2026.core: A. sensors, encoders, and other devices must be powered solely by the power regulation device they are connected to. Do not use outside power sources (e.g., custom circuits or a second hub) to power them,

s2027.core: B. power from a specific port may only power devices plugged into that exact port. Do not cross-wire power to other ports, and do not combine power from multiple ports into a single power bus/line,

s2036.core: We recommend teams always keep all control system device software up to date. Check the ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧FIRST⟦/2⟧ Tech Challenge Firmware Update Page⟦/1⟧ for release announcements and most recent software versions.

s2037.core: Due to unpredictable variations in Android software across different manufacturers and updates, the REV Control Hub is the only officially supported ROBOT CONTROLLER device. Teams choosing to use any other unsupported device (e.g., smartphones) are responsible for testing and verifying its compatibility, functionality, and performance.

s2044.core: The following are examples of allowed and disallowed devices:

s2045.core: Example 1: The Adafruit BNO055 Absolute Orientation Sensor is an IMU package with an onboard ARM Cortex-M0 based coprocessor to crunch sensor data and produce composite output. Its coprocessor contains software that is not intended by the manufacturer to be modified by users. This device is allowed.

s2046.core: Example 2: The SparkFun Optical Tracking Odometry Sensor is a laser and IMU tracking device that uses an onboard microcontroller to perform complex calculations and produce simplified results. SparkFun does provide the source code and toolchain for advanced users to modify/update the software, which is not permitted by this rule. s2051.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R703 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Smartphone Android devices used as a ROBOT CONTROLLER must connect to the REV Expansion Hub using USB. ⟦/2⟧If used as a ROBOT CONTROLLER, the smartphone Android device must be connected via its integrated USB port to a REV Expansion Hub with any combination of USB cables (including USB OTG cables) and/or USB hubs (powered or unpowered, with or without OTG integrated into the hub).

s2052.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧R704 ⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧* Use networks and bandwidth as directed. ⟦/4⟧Teams and ROBOTS must use Wi-Fi networks and bandwidth in a way that enables fair play and does not interfere with other teams or ARENA operations. Teams must abide by the following guidelines:

s2053.core: A. Teams may not use any other form of wireless communication, except those offered by the provided official tools, to communicate to, from, or within the ROBOT.

s2054.core: B. Teams may not interfere with the ROBOT networks. All communication signals must originate from only the ROBOT CONTROLLER device or the DRIVER STATION device using the ROBOT CONTROLLER Wi-Fi network. No other devices may attempt to connect to, interfere with, or alter the ROBOT CONTROLLER Wi-Fi network.

s2055.core: C. Ensure all programming laptops and other devices (other than the DRIVER STATION device) are disconnected from the ROBOT CONTROLLER Wi-Fi network during MATCH play.

s2056.core: D. Software with access to the ROBOT CONTROLLER Wi-Fi network must limit the amount of data being streamed (i.e., continuous transmission of data) over Wi-Fi. Software may only stream robot control data, debugging data, and telemetry to and from the ROBOT using the FTC Driver Station Application. Additional logging/streaming services, such as those hosted by third party plugins and tools such as FTC Dashboard, FTControl Panels, and others are prohibited. No continuous video stream is allowed.

s2057.core: E. Some events may assign Wi-Fi bands and/or channels to teams. If requested by event staff, teams must use the specific frequency band or channel on the day of the competition.

s2063.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧R706 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*Only specified modifications to core control system devices are permitted.⟦/3⟧ The DRIVER STATION device and software, Android-based ROBOT CONTROLLER device, main and secondary power switch(es), power regulation devices, fuses, and batteries shall not be tampered with, modified, or adjusted in any way (tampering includes drilling, cutting, machining, rewiring, disassembling, painting, removing enclosures and replacing with custom enclosures, etc.), with the following exceptions:

s2064.core: A. wires, cables, and signal lines may be connected via the standard connection points provided on the devices,

s2065.core: B. fasteners (including adhesives) may be used to attach devices to the OPERATOR CONSOLE or ROBOT or to secure cables to the device,

s2066.core: C. thermal interface material may be used to improve heat conduction,

s2067.core: D. labeling may be applied to indicate device identification, purpose, connectivity, functional performance, etc. as long as they do not cover labels or markings used to identify the product,

s2068.core: E. jumpers or switches may be moved to configure devices per the manufacturer’s manual,

s2069.core: F. device firmware may be updated with manufacturer supplied firmware,

s2070.core: G. integral wires on motor controllers and batteries may be cut, stripped, and/or connectorized,

s2071.core: H. devices except batteries may be repaired, provided the performance and specifications of the device after the repair are identical to those before the repair,

s2072.core: I. insulating material may be added to exposed conductors,

s2073.core: J. tape may be applied for debris protection, and

s2074.core: K. power switch mounting brackets can be modified or replaced.

s2075.core: Please note that while repairs are permitted, the allowance is independent of any manufacturer’s warranty. Teams make repairs at their own risk and should assume that any warranty or return options are forfeited. Repairs must be functionally equivalent to original device condition.

s2076.core: Be aware that diagnosing and repairing COMPONENTS such as these can be difficult.

s2077.core: For example, “repairs” that change connector types, include device footprint modifications, or provide mechanical enhancements, are prohibited. ⟦1/⟧

s2101.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R801 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*No Pneumatic Actuators, High-Speed Blowers, or Vacuums.⟦/2⟧ ROBOTS are restricted in their use of air in the following ways:

s2102.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧A. ⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ROBOTS may only use sealed, COTS closed-air systems which are pre-charged by the manufacturer (such as gas shocks),⟦/3⟧⟦/2⟧

s2103.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧B. ⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ROBOTS may not use any stored pressure COMPONENTS that are actuated by a device like a solenoid and/or are able to change their stable state,⟦/3⟧⟦/2⟧

s2104.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧C. ⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ROBOTS may not generate pressure or vacuum, ⟦/3⟧⟦/2⟧

s2105.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧D. ⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ROBOTS may not use any user-adjustable gas storage vessels, except air-filled (pneumatic) COTS wheels, and⟦/3⟧⟦/2⟧

s2106.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧E. ⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ROBOTS may not use any device which creates high-speed airflow, except cooling fans integrated into COTS computing devices.⟦/3⟧⟦/2⟧

s2107.core: The intent of this rule is that ROBOTS may not use pneumatic actuators, pressure or vacuum storage devices, compressors, vacuum generators, or air blowers, but they may use “closed air” systems which were sealed by their manufacturer. This includes items such as gas springs, and dampers.

s2108.core: Examples of a “device which creates high-speed airflow” include but are not limited to a fan designed to move SCORING ELEMENTS on the FIELD. ⟦1/⟧ High-speed flywheels or rollers used for manipulating SCORING ELEMENTS would not on their own be considered a high-speed airflow device.

s2110.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧R901 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*Use only a specified DRIVER STATION device.⟦/3⟧ The OPERATOR CONSOLE may only have one approved Android-based DRIVER STATION device connected and powered on. The OPERATOR CONSOLE must have at least one of the following:

s2112.core: B. Any Android Device with or without any combination of USB cables (including USB OTG cables) and/or USB hubs (powered or unpowered, with or without OTG integrated into the hub) for connecting one or more gamepads.

s2113.core: Due to unpredictable variations in Android software across different manufacturers and updates, the REV Driver Hub is the only officially supported DRIVER STATION device. Teams choosing to use any other unsupported device (e.g., smartphones) are responsible for testing and verifying its compatibility, functionality, and performance.

s2114.core: Teams who wish to have a spare DRIVER STATION device as part of their OPERATOR CONSOLE may do so as long as only one DRIVER STATION device is connected and powered on at a time.

s2115.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R902 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*The OPERATOR CONSOLE must make the touch screen accessible.⟦/2⟧ The OPERATOR CONSOLE, ⟦3⟧the set of COMPONENTS and MECHANISMS used by the DRIVE TEAM to relay commands to the ROBOT⟦/3⟧, must make the touch screen of the DRIVER STATION device accessible. The DRIVER STATION device must be positioned within the OPERATOR CONSOLE so that the screen display can be clearly seen during inspection and in a MATCH. The DRIVER STATION device touch screen must be functional without the requirement of additional aides (e.g., mouse) in order to be used.

s2116.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R903 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*OPERATOR CONSOLE physical requirements.⟦/2⟧ The OPERATOR CONSOLE, including all power sources (e.g., power banks), must not exceed a volume of 3ft wide, 1ft 6in deep and 2 ft tall (91.4 cm by 45.7 cm by 61.0 cm), excluding any items that are held or worn by the DRIVERS during the MATCH.

s2117.core: ⟦0⟧Also refer to ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R203⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧ for restrictions on designing OPERATOR CONSOLES for fair play and ARENA safety.⟦/2⟧

s2118.core: Please note that while there is no hard weight limit, OPERATOR CONSOLES that weigh more than 20 lbs. (~9 kg.) will invite extra scrutiny as they are likely to disrupt normal ARENA operations.

s2119.core: Teams who wish to have a spare external USB hub as part of the OPERATOR CONSOLE may do so as long as only one USB hub is connected at any time.

s2120.core: The intent of this rule is to allow teams to use a container to store, organize, and transport the DRIVER STATION device and support electronics. The OPERATOR CONSOLE rules are not intended to allow systems that function as a ROBOT cart or replace a competition-provided OPERATOR CONSOLE stand, table, etc.

s2121.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧R904 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*ROBOT application wireless communication only.⟦/2⟧ Other than the connection controlled by the ROBOT CONTROLLER app running on the ROBOT and the DRIVER STATION app running on the DRIVER STATION device, no other form of wireless communications shall be used to communicate to, from, or within the OPERATOR CONSOLE during a MATCH.

s2122.core: Examples of prohibited wireless systems include, but are not limited to, active wireless network cards, wireless gamepad communication, and Bluetooth devices.

s2125.core: Each ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ Tech Challenge competition is played in a head-to-head tournament format. Each tournament consists of 3 types of MATCHES: Practice MATCHES (not played at all events), Qualification MATCHES, and Playoff MATCHES.

s2126.core: - Practice MATCHES provide teams with an opportunity to operate their ROBOT on a competition FIELD prior to the start of the Qualification MATCHES.

s2127.core: - Qualification MATCHES allow each team to earn MATCH points and RANKING POINTS which determine their seeding position and may qualify them for participation in the Playoff MATCHES.

s2128.core: - Playoff MATCHES determine the event winning ALLIANCE.

s2129.core: These rules apply to all event types described in Section ⟦0⟧4⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧Advancement⟦/2⟧. Additional rules may apply to League Meets and League Tournaments as covered by Section ⟦3⟧14⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧ ⟦/4⟧⟦5⟧League Play Tournaments (L)⟦/5⟧.

s2131.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧T201 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Replays are allowed, but rare.⟦/2⟧ MATCH replays are only allowed in extreme circumstances due to an ARENA FAULT or for MATCHES which are stopped because FIELD STAFF anticipated FIELD damage or personal injury.

s2132.core: An ARENA FAULT is ⟦0⟧an error in ARENA operation⟦/0⟧ that includes, but is not limited to:

s2133.core: A. broken FIELD elements due to normal, expected gameplay,

s2134.core: B. broken FIELD elements due to ROBOT abuse of FIELD elements that affects the outcome of the MATCH for their opponents,

s2135.core: A broken FIELD element caused by ROBOT abuse that affects the outcome of the MATCH for their ALLIANCE is not an ARENA FAULT.

s2136.core: C. FIELD elements moving beyond normal tolerances (not as the result of ROBOT interaction),

s2137.core: D. Wide-spread wireless interference affecting multiple ROBOTS typically at the same time and on both ALLIANCES,

s2138.core: E. failure of the MATCH timer display, or

s2139.core: F. errors by FIELD STAFF (except those listed in Section ⟦0⟧10.8⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧Other Logistics⟦/2⟧).

s2140.core: If, as determined by the Head REFEREE, an ARENA FAULT occurs that affects the outcome of the MATCH and any team on the affected ALLIANCE desires a replay, the MATCH will be replayed. In addition, ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ Headquarters reserves the right to, with consultation of the Head REFEREE and FIELD STAFF, replay any MATCH in which an ARENA FAULT impacts the outcome of an event.

s2141.core: Unexpected ROBOT behaviors which are the fault of the team are not justifications for a replay. Conditions such as, but not limited to, low ROBOT battery, programming issues, or ROBOT mechanical problems are not grounds for a replay.

s2142.core: The outcome of the MATCH is affected if an error occurs that, as perceived by the Head REFEREE, changes which ALLIANCE would have won the MATCH and/or the assignment of RANKING POINTS.

s2143.core: The outcome of an event is affected if an error occurs that, in the judgement of ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ Headquarters, changes the assignment of RANKING POINTS or has a dramatic effect on points used for ranking criteria.

s2144.core: Note that an ARENA FAULT that does not affect MATCH outcome, as perceived by the Head REFEREE, does not lead to a MATCH replay. Examples include, but are not limited to:

s2145.core: A. ⟦0⟧a piece of FIELD plastic falls into the FIELD, far away from any human or ROBOT activity, and in such a way that it does not affect MATCH outcome,⟦/0⟧

s2146.core: B. ⟦0⟧delay in the playing of an ARENA sound, and ⟦/0⟧

s2147.core: ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧C. ⟦/1⟧⟦/0⟧⟦2⟧any adjustment or delay in assignment of a penalty or scoring achievement (including those made after the MATCH).⟦/2⟧

s2148.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧T202 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Replays will replicate the conditions of the original MATCH.⟦/2⟧ All reasonable effort is made to create the same conditions when replaying a MATCH caused by an ARENA FAULT or FIELD damage. This includes:

s2149.core: A. a ROBOT that was not present for the MATCH or DISABLED prior to the start of the original MATCH, which is to be replayed, is DISABLED for the replay MATCH

s2150.core: B. the same FIELD will be used unless otherwise deemed necessary by the Head REFEREE due to severity of FIELD damage

s2152.core: C. ROBOT and DRIVE TEAM starting locations and pre-loaded SCORING ELEMENTS do not need to be replicated when replaying a MATCH

s2153.core: While efforts will be made to replicate the same conditions of the original MATCH, there are environmental factors, such as changes to ambient lighting, that may be outside the control of the event.

s2154.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧⟦/4⟧⟦5⟧13.3 Clarifications on MATCH Play Results⟦/5⟧ (“Question Box”)

s2155.core: Each event will have one or more designated Question Boxes in the ARENA area. If a DRIVE TEAM has a question about a MATCH, the FIELD, etc., they may send up to two representatives wearing a DRIVE TEAM badge to their corresponding Question Box. Depending on timing, the Head REFEREE or FTA may postpone any requested discussion until the end of the subsequent MATCH.

s2156.core: Technical questions regarding FIELD or ROBOT operation are addressed by the FTA, and additional team members are invited to participate in these conversations if necessary. If a DRIVE TEAM needs clarification on a ruling or MATCH results, per ⟦0⟧T301⟦/0⟧, up to two representatives should address the Head REFEREE after the MATCH results have been shown.

s2157.core: While the ⟦0⟧FIRST⟦/0⟧ event management software tracks quantities of MINOR and MAJOR FOULS, ⟦1⟧FIRST⟦/1⟧ instructs REFEREES to not self-track details about MINOR FOULS and MAJOR FOULS; as a result, we do not expect REFEREES to recall details about what MINOR FOULS and MAJOR FOULS were made, when they occurred, and against whom.

s2158.core: Any reasonable question is fair game in the Question Box, and Head REFEREES will make good faith efforts to provide helpful feedback (e.g., how/why certain FOULS are being called, why a particular ROBOT may be susceptible to certain FOULS based on its design or gameplay, how specific rules are being called or interpreted), but please know that they may not be able to supply specific details.

s2159.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧T301 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*Head REFEREE interactions.⟦/3⟧ A team may only address the Head REFEREE with a maximum of 2 people, 1 of which must be a STUDENT.

s2160.core: Violation: The Head REFEREE will not address additional, non-compliant team members or peripheral conversations.

s2161.core: Some events may restrict ARENA access to members of the DRIVE TEAM. Team members are permitted to swap buttons within their team as needed to access the Question Box.

s2162.core: ⟦0⟧As much as possible, the STUDENT should be an active participant in the conversation. Teams should not record interactions without consent (see ⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧E116⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧).⟦/2⟧

s2163.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧T302 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*MATCH questions must be timely. ⟦/2⟧If a team would like to clarify or dispute the results of a MATCH using the process per ⟦3⟧T301⟦/3⟧ they must present their STUDENT representative in the Question Box in a timely manner as outlined below:

s2164.core: A. questions regarding events in a Qualification MATCH may be asked at any time before ALLIANCE selection begins, or within 5 minutes of the last Qualification MATCH at events without Playoff MATCHES, and

s2165.core: B. questions regarding events in a Playoff MATCH must be asked before the start of the next Playoff round or, for the last Playoff MATCH, immediately following the MATCH.

s2166.core: Please keep in mind that our REFEREES are human, and the more time has passed between the MATCH in question, the less likely they are to remember the details of a specific MATCH. It is best to ask for clarification or to dispute the results of a MATCH within 3 MATCHES.

s2167.core: Teams are encouraged to ask questions as soon as possible. Questions asked more than 5 minutes after the last Playoff MATCH will likely not be addressed.

s2168.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧T303 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*Keep questions factual and constructive. ⟦/2⟧Teams coming to the Question Box should think through their requests in advance and are encouraged to have relevant references to rules or the ⟦3⟧Q&A website⟦/3⟧ available to aid discussions.

s2169.core: There should be no negative implications for teams using the Question Box to advocate for themselves, but everyone should keep in mind it can be a high stress situation for team youth and for volunteers alike and it is important to remember ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧FIRST⟦/2⟧ Core Values⟦/1⟧ during these discussions. ⟦3/⟧ At some events, MATCH results may be available on the ⟦4⟧FTC-Events⟦/4⟧ page.

s2171.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧T401 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*The Head REFEREE has ultimate and final authority regarding gameplay during the event.⟦/3⟧⟦4⟧⟦5⟧ The Head REFEREE may receive ⟦/5⟧⟦/4⟧input from additional sources, e.g., ⟦6⟧FIRST⟦/6⟧ personnel, FTA, Event Director, Program Delivery Partner, and other event staff. The Head REFEREE rulings are final. No event staff, including the Head REFEREE, will review video, photos, artistic renderings, etc. of any MATCH, from any source, under any circumstances.

s2172.core: A. When issuing a RED CARD or YELLOW CARD the Head REFEREE must record the rule violation.

s2173.core: B. Event Directors and Program Delivery Partners may not overrule a Head REFEREE decision.

s2174.core: C. ⟦0⟧Framework of Behaviors⟦/0⟧ and⟦1⟧ ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧Competition Integrity Contract (CIC)⟦/2⟧ violations may involve escalation beyond the Head REFEREE’S initial ruling.

s2175.core: D. Every Qualification and Playoff MATCH must be observed by a certified Head REFEREE. Head REFEREES may only watch 1 MATCH at a time.

s2176.core: Rules in this manual are written for ⟦2⟧human⟦/2⟧ Head REFEREES to enforce. Some have clear unambiguous criteria which can be easily checked, but other rules will rely on human judgement. Head REFEREES are asked to make the best call they can in the moment with what they or other REFEREES observed during the MATCH.

s2177.core: When there is an ambiguous situation or controversial call it is human instinct to wonder what was the “right call” or “what-if...” – for the purposes of ⟦2⟧FIRST⟦/2⟧ Tech Challenge gameplay, the right call is the one that was made in good faith by the Head REFEREE with the information they had available at the time.

s2178.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧T402 ⟦/4⟧⟦/3⟧⟦5⟧*Only REFEREES can declare a ROBOT DISABLED. ⟦/5⟧A ROBOT is only considered DISABLED once a REFEREE has declared the ROBOT DISABLED during a MATCH. A ROBOT may only be DISABLED as a consequence of a rule violation. If a REFEREE DISABLES a ROBOT, the REFEREE may instruct the team to drive the ROBOT to a specific neutral position on the FIELD before DISABLING.

Issues outside of specific gameplay rules which are under the authority of the Head REFEREE per ⟦/5⟧⟦/4⟧⟦7⟧T401⟦/7⟧⟦8⟧⟦9⟧ are at the discretion of the Event Director such as, but not limited to:⟦/9⟧⟦/8⟧

s2180.core: A. venue access as published via the public schedule,

s2181.core: B. pit sizes and utility access,

s2183.core: D. team registration and competition eligibility, and

s2184.core: E. team conduct away from the ARENA.

s2185.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧T404 ⟦/2⟧⟦3⟧*All competition FIELDS at an event must be consistent with each other. ⟦/3⟧Events which have multiple competition FIELDS (as indicated by the MATCH schedule Figure 13‑1) will be consistent with each other. Examples of set-up which must be considered includes, but is not limited to:

s2186.core: A. elevation of the FIELD off the floor,

s2189.core: D. FIELD TILE size and type.

s2190.core: Other FIELDS (e.g., practice FIELDS) at the event do not need to be consistent with each other or competition FIELDS.

s2191.core: ⟦0⟧⟦/0⟧⟦1⟧T405 ⟦/1⟧⟦2⟧*During optional FIELD measurement and calibration time(s) ROBOTS may not practice on the FIELD.⟦/2⟧ During any period when the ARENA is open for measurement, ROBOTS may run OpModes but cannot move the ROBOT (e.g., CHASSIS) under its own power around the FIELD.

s2192.core: Violation: VERBAL WARNING. YELLOW CARD if subsequent violations occur during the event.

The specific time that the FIELD is open will be communicated to teams at the event. Teams may bring specific questions or comments to the Head REFEREE or FTA.

s2194.core: Allowed activities during ROBOT calibration and measurement time(s) include:

s2197.core: C. ⟦0⟧ROBOT may operate or extend MECHANISMS outside the ROBOT CHASSIS,⟦/0⟧

s2199.core: E. ⟦0⟧ROBOT may be connected to programming laptops and other devices,⟦/0⟧

s2200.core: F. ⟦0⟧team members may be on the FIELD with the ROBOT,⟦/0⟧

s2201.core: G. ⟦0⟧team members may manually move the ROBOT to multiple positions around the FIELD (e.g., without driving the ROBOT under its own power), and⟦/0⟧

s2202.core: H. ⟦0⟧team members or ROBOTS may measure the FIELD with tools (e.g., tape measures) or sensors.⟦/0⟧

s2203.core: Activities not allowed during ROBOT calibration and measurement time(s) include:

s2204.core: I. ⟦0⟧ROBOT CHASSIS may not move under its own power around the FIELD (i.e., “driving” as part of AUTO or TELEOP),⟦/0⟧

s2205.core: J. ⟦0⟧ROBOT may not LAUNCH SCORING ELEMENTS, and⟦/0⟧
